title: Reaction rates and equilibrium
lede: Why food lasts longer in the fridge, how a catalytic converter and the DEF in a diesel truck clean exhaust, and the principle that predicts which way a reaction will shift when you push on it.

sections.md:
## Collision theory
For molecules to react, they must **collide** with enough energy (the **activation energy**) and in the right orientation. Anything that increases effective collisions speeds a reaction up.

| Factor | Effect | Why | Everyday example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Temperature** ↑ | faster | molecules move faster and hit harder | food spoils faster outside the fridge |
| **Concentration** ↑ | faster | more particles, more collisions | pure oxygen makes things burn fiercely |
| **Surface area** ↑ | faster | more exposed particles | powdered sugar dissolves faster than a cube |
| **Catalyst** added | faster | provides a lower-energy pathway | enzymes; catalytic converters |

A rough rule of thumb: many reactions go about **twice as fast** for every **10 °C** rise.

## Catalysts
A **catalyst** speeds a reaction by lowering the activation energy, and it's **not used up**.

- **Enzymes** are biological catalysts (from the biochemistry lesson).
- A car's **catalytic converter** uses metals like platinum, palladium and rhodium to turn toxic carbon monoxide, unburned fuel and nitrogen oxides into less harmful CO₂, water and nitrogen.
- Modern diesel trucks use **selective catalytic reduction (SCR)**: **diesel exhaust fluid (DEF)**, a urea solution, is sprayed into the exhaust, and over a catalyst it converts **nitrogen oxides (NOx)** into **nitrogen and water**. That's why the DEF tank matters.

sections.q: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by…
sections.why: A lower-energy path; it's not used up.

sections.md:
## Reversible reactions and equilibrium
Many reactions can run **both ways**, written with ⇌.

At first the forward reaction is fast. As products build up, the reverse reaction speeds up. Eventually both run at the **same rate**: **dynamic equilibrium**. The reactions haven't stopped; they're balanced, so the **amounts** stay constant.

*Picture a busy store:* people enter and leave constantly, but if the rates match, the number inside stays the same.

The **equilibrium constant K** compares products to reactants at equilibrium:
- **K ≫ 1**: mostly products at equilibrium
- **K ≪ 1**: mostly reactants

## Le Chatelier's principle
When you disturb a system at equilibrium, it **shifts to counteract the change**.

The classic example is the **Haber process**, which makes ammonia for fertilizer (and helps feed a large share of the world's population):

**N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃ + heat** (exothermic)

| Change | System shifts | Why |
|---|---|---|
| add N₂ or H₂ | → right (more NH₃) | uses up the added reactant |
| remove NH₃ | → right | replaces what was removed |
| raise pressure | → right | 2 gas molecules on the right vs 4 on the left: fewer molecules relieves pressure |
| raise temperature | ← left | heat acts like a product; the system absorbs the added heat |
| add a catalyst | **no shift** | reaches equilibrium faster, same position |

That creates a real-world trade-off: lower temperatures give **more** ammonia but form it **slowly**. Industry compromises with moderate temperature, high pressure, a catalyst, and constant removal of ammonia.

sections.q: For N₂ + 3 H₂ ⇌ 2 NH₃, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium…
sections.why: Toward fewer gas molecules: 2 on the right vs 4 on the left.

sections.title: Equilibrium in your blood
sections.problem: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. During hard sparring, your muscles release CO₂ into the blood. Which way does it shift, and what does your body do?
steps: More CO₂ (a reactant) → the equilibrium shifts **right**.
More H⁺ forms → blood becomes slightly more acidic.
Your brain senses this and makes you **breathe harder**, blowing off CO₂ to shift it back left.
sections.answer: Heavy breathing after a round isn't just about getting oxygen in. It's Le Chatelier in your bloodstream: dumping CO₂ to control blood acidity.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Equilibrium doesn't mean equal amounts.** It means equal **rates**.
- **Catalysts don't shift equilibrium.** They just get there faster.
- **Temperature is the only factor that changes K itself.** Concentration and pressure shift the position without changing K.
- **Faster ≠ more.** Rate (how fast) and equilibrium (how far) are different questions.

forward and reverse rates are equal

For the exothermic Haber process, why don't factories run it at low temperature to maximize ammonia?
options: Low temperature gives more ammonia at equilibrium but makes the reaction too slow
practice.why: Classic trade-off between **how far** (equilibrium favors low T) and **how fast** (rate favors high T).
